name: KubeVirt
summary: Adds virtual machines to Kubernetes as ordinary resources, so VMs and containers share one cluster, one API and one set of tools.
intro: KubeVirt is an add-on that teaches an existing Kubernetes cluster to run full virtual machines. It adds custom resources: a `VirtualMachine` you can stop and start while its disks persist, and the `VirtualMachineInstance` that represents it while it runs. When an instance is created, `virt-controller` makes a normal pod for it, and Kubernetes schedules that pod like any other. On the chosen node, the `virt-handler` DaemonSet tells the pod’s `virt-launcher` container to start the VM, which it does through a libvirt daemon inside the pod running QEMU with KVM. The VM process therefore lives inside the pod’s cgroups and namespaces, and Kubernetes handles scheduling, networking and storage while KubeVirt adds only the virtualisation.

Disks come from persistent volume claims, or from a “container disk”, a VM image shipped in a container registry. The companion Containerized Data Importer (CDI) adds a `DataVolume` resource that fills a volume from a URL, a registry, an upload or a clone of another volume. A running VM can live-migrate to another node, started by creating a `VirtualMachineInstanceMigration` object, as long as its volumes are shared (ReadWriteMany). Red Hat started KubeVirt in 2016 and builds OpenShift Virtualization on it; SUSE, NVIDIA, Cloudflare and CoreWeave are among its listed users. It is a CNCF incubating project, reached version 1.0 in July 2023 and now releases three times a year in step with Kubernetes.
strengths: One control plane for VMs and containers: the same `kubectl`, RBAC, GitOps, monitoring and storage classes for both
Runs Windows guests and other workloads that don’t fit in a container, such as CI runners or virtual desktops, next to containers
Live migration, snapshots, VM export and disk import through standard Kubernetes objects
Backed by several vendors: OpenShift Virtualization (Red Hat), SUSE’s products and others ship it
limits: Nodes need hardware virtualisation (bare metal or nested virtualisation); a software-emulation fallback exists for testing
Live migration needs ReadWriteMany storage and doesn’t work with every network binding
More moving parts: a VM is a pod plus a libvirt and QEMU stack, and features such as disk import live in separate add-ons like CDI
These are full VMs with their own operating systems to patch, not lightweight sandboxes for containers

story: By 2016 containers and Kubernetes were becoming the standard way to run new software, but most companies still had large estates of virtual machines that couldn’t easily be rewritten. Running both meant two platforms, two teams and two sets of tools. At the end of 2016 engineers at Red Hat asked whether VMs could run inside containers and be deployed by Kubernetes.

Their answer was to extend Kubernetes rather than build beside it: VMs became custom resources, each VM ran inside a pod, and Kubernetes kept doing the scheduling, networking and storage. The first release, v0.1.0, came in December 2017. KubeVirt joined the CNCF as a sandbox project in September 2019 and moved to incubating in April 2022.

Version 1.0 shipped in July 2023, after the project switched from monthly releases to three a year to match Kubernetes. KubeVirt now sits under OpenShift Virtualization and products from SUSE, Oracle and others.

choices.why: Wrapping each VM in a pod lets the existing scheduler, network plugins and volume drivers handle it, so KubeVirt only adds the virtualisation and not a second cluster manager.

choices.choice: Extend the API with custom resources
choices.why: Defining VMs as Kubernetes objects, with controllers that reconcile them, means users manage VMs through the same API and tools as everything else.
Instead of writing a new hypervisor, each `virt-launcher` pod runs the mature libvirt and QEMU stack, which brings broad guest support, including Windows, and features such as live migration.
